description: Space Players III is coming back!
summary:
With the goal of identifying locations on Earth that serve as analogues for permanent lunar bases and Mars, we developed a machine learning system capable of aggregating and correlating compositional data from the soil of the Moon and Mars with the compositions found in the Paraná Igneous Province, in Brazil. 

Our solution directly addresses the challenge by identifying the precise locations and the specific types of local soil that most closely resemble those found at space lava tubes, so that, in this way, the astronaut’s research can be more efficient, with a focus on maintaining safety and managing the high cost associated with these missions. 

Our system aims, primarily, to change the way space missions are planned, as it is based on studies in an unexplored location that has much to contribute in the exploration of analog environments in order to innovate and transform the methods used by these scientists and engineers.
details:
Our project identified and validated the Paraná Igneous Province (PIP) as a terrestrial analogue for lunar and Martian lava tubes. Firstly, we collected the geochemical compositions of samples extracted from the PIP using the GEOROC Database. Then, we identified the composition of High-Ti and Low-Ti samples from the Moon and the composition of Martian Regolith rocks. We extracted these from literature planetary reference sources: Lunar Sourcebook: A User's Guide to the Moon (Heiken, G. H.) and Mojave Mars simulant—Characterization of a new geologic Mars analog (Peters, G.H.).

With that, we developed a StandardScaler Machine Learning code that returned to us a similarity score based on the distance of a Paraná sample to a reference one in a 8 dimension plane, referent to all of the main eight oxides selected to be features. They were: 

  • SiO2: SÍlica
  • TiO2: Titania
  • Al2O3: Alumina
  • MnO: Manganese oxide
  • MgO: Magnesia
  • CaO: Calcium oxide
  • Na2O: Sodium oxide
  • K2O: Potassium oxide

We used Python (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn) in VS Code and Jupyter Notebook. We also used Google Gemini to help debug our code.

Most of the Paraná basalt samples had a similarity score higher than 90% with one of the references, but to increase precision in our data, we set the minimum valid score at 95%. With that, 6 samples were found to be >95% similar to Martian regolith and 16 to the low-Ti lunar basalt. Even though there are differences between the high and low-Ti terrestrial basalts, the weight percentage of Titanium in it is still considerably lower than the weight percentage of the Lunar high-Ti sample, making no sample have a similarity score higher than 95%

With the data of the valid analogues uploaded in a csv. file, we created an interactive map of their locations using Google Earth Pro: https://earth.google.com/earth/d/1NUJ80XvggEY87U5gNLOkbBPO6545Gcs8?usp=sharing

We decided to focus on the PIP due to many factors. First, because it’s a rich, yet unexplored region in South America that still has much to teach us about our planet and even other ones. There’s still a lack of formal exploration and characterization of its terrains, which made finding the data a hard process. Secondly, not only are the rock compositions similar, but the shapes and textures of the PIP formations are perfect for mimicking different environments on the Moon and Mars. There are cliffs, steep slopes, caves, craters, and even ancient lava tubes.

At the PIP, rovers' locomotion and autonomy, resource extraction, drilling and anchoring tools, and biophysical hypotheses can all be tested. We hope that those experiments conducted in Brazilian soil can increase the safety, budget control and efficiency of space missions. However, it’s important to note that most of our analysed locations are not suitable for spacewalk simulations or full-sized habitat installations, due to them not being very isolated or being cliffs/slopes.

Because of the hackathon's timeframe, our next steps were designed conceptually, though we didn't have time to code them yet. First, we want to build an Interactive Web Database that includes additional rock traits, like density, rugosity, and scarp angles, where researchers can upload their own datasets and choose metric weights to get similarity scores for targets like Mare Tranquillitatis or Arsia Mons. Second, we plan to develop an AI Image Recognition System trained on the PIP’s basalt photos to help rovers autonomously check the structural stability of lava tubes and steep craters, making ground decisions faster.

We hope to bring more attention to the emerging South American Space Industry and to spread the richness and diversity of Brazilian land.

I hope you enjoy our project!
